## Global Instructions

### Commit message conventions

When generating Git commit messages, use Conventional Commits.

Format:

<type>(<scope>): <description>

Allowed types:

- feat
- fix
- refactor
- test
- docs
- chore
- build
- ci
- perf
- style

Rules:

- Write all commit messages in English.
- Infer scope from changed files.
- Keep subject under 72 characters.
- Use the concise imperative mood.
- Do not use vague messages like "update files" or "misc changes".

### Domain language

When a domain model exists, use the canonical terms from the relevant `CONTEXT.md` in all communication and project work. If `CONTEXT-MAP.md` exists, use it to select the applicable glossary. Explicitly resolve any terminology conflicts before proceeding.

### Process discipline

Reaching the expected result is not enough; reach it through the process the repository expects. A result reached by an improvised process is hard to review and repeat, and usually drops constraints the process exists to protect.

#### Read the skills that apply

- When a skill available in the current context clearly covers the situation, read it in full, with the resources it points to, before the first action it governs.
- Treat a description as routing only. It carries none of the skill's constraints, formats, ordering, decision criteria, or failure handling.
- A skill is present because default behavior was judged insufficient. Assume it encodes details you cannot infer, and do not let familiarity with the topic replace reading it.
- Read each skill that governs a distinct part of the work, and resolve conflicts between them explicitly.
- Do not use every available skill. A loosely related skill only adds noise; the obligation covers an unmistakable match.

#### Follow OpenSpec instructions

- When a repository uses OpenSpec, its instructions, schema, and templates are deliberate human decisions about the path to a result, not reference material for after the fact.
- Read them before creating or changing an artifact, and follow their stages, structure, and syntax.
- Validate with the project's tooling, such as `openspec validate`.
- Do not skip, reorder, or compress stages because you expect the same outcome without them.
- Deviate only when a human directs it or an instruction cannot be satisfied, and state what you deviated from and why.

### Production readiness

Build every feature to production-ready standards from its first implementation.

Do not use labels such as MVP, prototype, test release, or initial version to justify deferring essential engineering work. Every delivered capability must include an appropriate level of:

- correctness;
- reliability;
- security;
- maintainability;
- observability;
- test coverage;
- failure handling.

When time or resources constrain delivery, reduce the number of capabilities in scope. Do not lower the engineering quality of the capabilities that remain.

## Repository purpose

This repository exists exclusively as a registry and authoring workspace for reusable skills and AI agents that are installed in other repositories.

Use this repository only to create new reusable skills and agents or to edit existing ones.

Most skills maintained here are designed to operate on other repositories and cannot be meaningfully applied to this repository itself. Do not invoke a skill here merely because it is present in the registry. A skill may be applied within this repository only when it is repository-agnostic and its purpose is relevant to creating or maintaining the registry, its skills, or its agents.
